From Middle English cave, borrowed from Old French cave, from Latin cava (“cavity”), from cavus (“hollow”). Cognate with Tocharian B kor (“throat”), Albanian cup (“odd, uneven”), Ancient Greek κύαρ (kúar, “eye of needle, earhole”), Old Armenian սոր (sor, “hole”), Sanskrit शून्य (śūnya, “empty, barren, zero”). Displaced native Old English sċræf. More at cavum, cavus and cage.

ety.text: Learned borrowing from Latin cavē, second-person singular present active imperative of caveō (“to beware”). Used at Eton College, Berkshire.

senses.d: A large, naturally-occurring cavity formed underground or in the face of a cliff or a hillside.
ex: We found a cave on the mountainside where we could take shelter.

senses.d: A hole, depression, or gap in earth or rock, whether natural or man-made.
ex: Every boy at one time or another has dug a cave; I suppose because ages and ages ago his ancestors had to live in caves, […]

senses.d: A storage cellar, especially for wine or cheese.
ex: This wine has been aged in our cave for thirty years.

senses.d: A place of retreat, such as a man cave.
ex: My room was a cozy cave where I could escape from my family.

senses.d: A naturally-occurring cavity in bedrock which is large enough to be entered by an adult.
ex: It was not strictly a cave, but a narrow fissure in the rock.

senses.d: A shielded area where nuclear experiments can be carried out.
ex: These potential radiation fields or radioactive material levels may be the result of normal operations (ie, radiation in a target cave) […]

senses.d: Debris, particularly broken rock, which falls into a drill hole and interferes with drilling.
ex: […] the casing can then be placed in the hole without encountering any cave and core drilling in rock can begin.

senses.d: A collapse or cave-in.
The vagina.
A group that breaks from a larger political party or faction on a particular issue.
ex: Without joining the cave, Hyde had abstained both in December 1956 and May 1957.

senses.d: To surrender.
To collapse.
ex: First the braces buckled, then the roof began to cave, then we ran.

senses.d: To hollow out or undermine.
ex: The levee has been severely caved by the river current.

senses.d: To engage in the recreational exploration of caves.
In room-and-pillar mining, to extract a deposit of rock by breaking down a pillar which had been holding it in place.
ex: The deposit is caved by knocking out the posts.

senses.d: To work over tailings to dress small pieces of marketable ore.
ex: As an indication of the miners' desperation in these years, the free miners of Wensley lowered themselves to caving for scraps of ore.

senses.d: To dwell in a cave.
ex: although perhaps / It may be heard at court that such as we / Cave here, hunt here, are outlaws, and in time / May make some stronger head

senses.d: look out!; beware!
